faq.q: Was Manhattan really bought for 24 dollars?
faq.a: The only surviving record is a 1626 letter reporting a purchase for goods worth 60 guilders. The 24 dollar figure is a nineteenth century conversion, no deed survives, and the letter says nothing about beads.

faq.q: What does Mannahatta mean?
faq.a: It is the Munsee name recorded for the island in the log of Hudson's 1609 voyage. The usual reading is island of many hills, but the etymology is not settled.

faq.q: Why is Wall Street called Wall Street?
faq.a: In 1653 Peter Stuyvesant had a wooden wall built across the island at the northern edge of New Amsterdam against a feared English attack. The road along it became Wall Street, and the wall came down in 1699.

faq.q: When did New Amsterdam become New York?
faq.a: Stuyvesant surrendered to an English fleet on September 8, 1664, and the town was renamed for the Duke of York. The Dutch held it again for a year in 1673 and 1674 before giving it up for good.

title: The High Line and the Rewilded City
summary: The West Side freight line, Friends of the High Line, the park's opening on June 9, 2009, Hudson Yards and the Vessel, and Little Island in 2021.

body.p: Through the nineteenth century the New York Central Railroad ran freight trains at street level down the West Side avenues. The trains killed so many people that the papers called the route Death Avenue, and the railroad hired men on horseback, the West Side Cowboys, to ride ahead of each train waving a flag.

The West Side Improvement, agreed among the city, the state and the railroad in 1929, lifted the tracks off the street. The elevated freight line opened in 1934. It ran from 34th Street south to a terminal at Spring Street, about 30 feet above the ground, and it passed through the middle of the blocks rather than over the avenue, so that trains could roll into the upper floors of warehouses and the Nabisco factory that is now Chelsea Market.

Trucks took the freight. The southern section was torn down in the 1960s. The last train ran in 1980, carrying three carloads of frozen turkeys. For 20 years the structure stood empty over the Meatpacking District and West Chelsea, and a meadow of self seeded grasses, trees and wildflowers grew in the ballast. Property owners under it pressed for demolition, and in the 1990s the city signed papers to tear it down.

In 1999 two residents of the neighborhood, Joshua David and Robert Hammond, met at a community board meeting and founded Friends of the High Line to save it. Photographs by Joel Sternfeld of the wild meadow on the tracks made the case in public. The Bloomberg administration reversed course in 2002, and the city won federal approval to convert the line to a trail in 2005.

The design team was James Corner Field Operations with Diller Scofidio + Renfro and the Dutch planting designer Piet Oudolf. The plan kept the rails in the paving, replanted the self seeded meadow as a designed one, and pulled the walkway through the buildings the trains had passed through.

The first section, from Gansevoort Street to West 20th Street, opened on June 9, 2009. The second, to West 30th Street, opened on June 8, 2011. The third, around the West Side rail yards to 34th Street, opened on September 21, 2014, and the Spur over Tenth Avenue at 30th Street opened in 2019. The park runs about 1.45 miles. Friends of the High Line operates it under a license from the Parks Department and raises most of its budget.

The park drew millions of visitors a year and a wall of new towers along it. Cities around the world copied it. Critics noted that the rents under it rose with the visitor count, and that the neighborhood the founders had wanted to keep changed anyway.

The rail yards the third section wraps around became Hudson Yards, built on a platform over the working tracks, the largest private real estate development in the country. Its first phase opened on March 15, 2019. At its center stood the Vessel, a 150 foot structure of 154 interconnected flights of stairs designed by Thomas Heatherwick. The Shed, an arts center whose outer shell rolls out over the plaza on rails, opened the following month.
The Vessel closed in 2021 after a series of deaths by suicide from its upper levels and reopened in 2024 with higher barriers and steel mesh on the climbable levels.

South of the High Line's start, on the site of Pier 54 in Hudson River Park, Little Island opened on May 21, 2021. Heatherwick Studio designed it with the landscape architects MNLA. It rests on 132 concrete pots shaped like tulips, on piles driven into the river, and holds a 2.4 acre park with a 687 seat amphitheater. Barry Diller and Diane von Furstenberg paid for most of it and committed to fund its upkeep. The Hudson River Park Trust owns the site.

Together the High Line, Hudson Yards and Little Island turned a working waterfront the city had abandoned into a strip of parks, and did it mostly with private money. The rewilded city is a built one.

The High Line room of the museum hangs the joggers, the gardeners and the tourists of the park. The Vessel room and the Shed room hold Hudson Yards, its climbers, its ushers and its cranes. The Little Island room holds the amphitheater crowd and the river. The atlas at map.html pins each character to a pier or a block on the West Side.
